title: Alaska Earthquake of 1964
summary: Josh and Chuck cover the 1964 Good Friday earthquake in Alaska, a magnitude 9.2 megathrust quake on March 27, 1964, the second largest ever recorded. They explain megathrust subduction at the Alaska-Aleutian Subduction Zone, the seiche waves felt across the US and abroad, the tsunamis that killed most victims (including Chenega and Port Valdez), liquefaction and land subsidence in Anchorage, the relocation of Valdez, and how the quake helped confirm plate tectonics and birth paleoseismology and land-slide tsunami science. They discuss a fungus (Cryptococcus gattii) carried inland by tsunami, the rise of seismograph networks and building codes, the 2018 Anchorage quake and 2002 Denali fault quake near the Trans-Alaska Pipeline. The episode ends with a promotional segment about the hosts' Virgin Cruises "Stuff at Sea" voyage to Bermuda.

segments.title: Opening banter and earthquake anecdotes
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the episode on the 1964 Alaska earthquake and trade personal earthquake experiences, including Chuck feeling a quake in Central Florida from Cuba.

segments.title: Overview of the Good Friday earthquake
segments.summary: The quake was magnitude 9.2, second largest recorded behind Chile's 9.5 in 1960. It killed about 131 people, with roughly 15 from the shaking itself and most from tsunamis.

segments.title: Megathrust earthquakes and subduction
segments.summary: Explanation of how megathrust quakes occur when a heavier plate subducts beneath a lighter one and locks until it slips, and that most of the largest recorded quakes are megathrust events.

segments.title: Alaska-Aleutian Subduction Zone and rupture size
segments.summary: The quake occurred at the Alaska-Aleutian Subduction Zone; the rupture area was about 500 by 125 miles and land moved tens of feet within seconds.

segments.title: Timing and seiche waves across the world
segments.summary: The quake struck March 27, 1964 around 5:36 pm and lasted about four minutes. Water level changes were recorded across US states and seiche waves reached Australia, South Africa, and the Gulf of Mexico, where boats sank off Louisiana.

segments.title: Coastline changes and drowned forests
segments.summary: Coastal land rose up to forty feet in some places and dropped in others, changing the coastline by as much as fifty feet. Entire forest stands dropped into the ocean.

segments.title: Tsunamis and casualties
segments.summary: Most deaths came from tsunamis, including a wave reaching about 200 feet and deaths as far away as California. Chenega was washed away within four minutes, with 23 of 68 residents dying.

segments.title: Port Valdez fires and soil liquefaction
segments.summary: Port Valdez was hit by tsunamis, with 32 deaths and burning oil tankers. Because the town sat on sand and gravel, liquefaction swallowed parts of it.

segments.title: Anchorage landslides and subsidence
segments.summary: Triggered landslides in Anchorage and the business district sank about nine feet, with nearby areas dropping up to twenty feet.

segments.title: Aftermath, disaster declaration, and communication
segments.summary: Lyndon Johnson declared Alaska a major disaster area; roads and phone lines were down. Damage was about three billion dollars in today's dollars. Shipping lanes were redrawn and Valdez was relocated about four miles away.

segments.title: Hiking the old Valdez site
segments.summary: Chuck notes that the original Valdez townsite can be hiked, with street signs and plaques marking former locations.

segments.title: Role in confirming plate tectonics
segments.summary: The quake provided evidence that plate tectonics explained the land uplift, subsidence and tsunamis, at a time when the theory was still debated; USGS scientists studied the site.

segments.title: Buried forests and paleoseismology
segments.summary: Scientists found older buried land plants beneath the sunken forests, showing such events had happened before. This birthed paleoseismology and led to searches for similar records at the Cascadia subduction zone.

segments.title: Landslide tsunamis in fjords
segments.summary: Tsunamis hit some coastal areas within minutes because quake-triggered underwater landslides from glacier-fed fjord sediment produced waves, a new concept called landslide tsunami.

segments.title: Cryptococcus gattii fungus spread by tsunami
segments.summary: A fungus native to tropics, Cryptococcus gattii, arrived in the Pacific Northwest via ship ballast around 1900 and was spread inland by the 1964 tsunami; it later caused infections in the 1990s, traced by epidemiologists.

segments.title: Building codes, seismographs, and hazard maps
segments.summary: The quake led to better building codes and more seismograph stations; the nuclear arms race drove early seismograph deployment. Later networks and the National Seismic Hazard Map followed, including the USArray project.

segments.title: Tsunami warning and later Alaska quakes
segments.summary: Tsunami warning systems improved and the National Tsunami Warning Center was established. Hosts mention the 2018 Anchorage quake (magnitude 7.0, no deaths) and a larger 2021 quake of 8.2 in a remote area.

segments.title: Trans-Alaska Pipeline and Denali fault
segments.summary: The 2002 magnitude 7.9 Denali fault earthquake did not cause much damage to the Trans-Alaska Pipeline, which crosses the fault.

segments.title: Listener mail skipped; Stuff at Sea cruise promo
segments.summary: Hosts skip listener mail and promote an October cruise to Bermuda with Virgin Cruises, with a live show and onboard events.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts sign off and give the listener email address.
